name: Mao Zedong
info: Mao Zedong was a Chinese revolutionary and political theorist who led the Chinese Communist Party to power, founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and was its paramount leader until his death in 1976.

facts.born: 26 December 1893, near Shaoshan village in Hunan, under the Qing dynasty; son of Mao Yichang, a formerly impoverished peasant who had become one of Shaoshan's wealthiest farmers, and Wen Qimei
facts.died: 9 September 1976, shortly after midnight, aged 82, after years of lung and heart ailments and three heart attacks that year
facts.role: Founding member of the Chinese Communist Party (1921); Chairman of the Military Commission (from 1935); Chairman of the Communist Party (from 1943); paramount leader of the People's Republic of China (1949-1976) and its President until 1959
facts.known: The Long March; founding the People's Republic of China; land reform and the campaigns against 'counter-revolutionaries'; the Great Leap Forward and the famine that followed; the Cultural Revolution; Mao Zedong Thought and the theory of people's war; the Little Red Book; poetry and calligraphy

t: Mao rose from a peasant family in Hunan to become a founding member of the Chinese Communist Party, built its Red Army on the peasantry and guerrilla warfare, and took the party's leadership during the Long March of 1934-1935.

After defeating the Nationalist government he proclaimed the People's Republic of China in 1949 and led land reform, industrialisation and a series of campaigns against those the party named its enemies.

Under his rule tens of millions died, most in the famine that followed the Great Leap Forward of 1958-1962, and millions were persecuted in the Cultural Revolution; he is also credited with gains in literacy, women's status, health and China's standing as a power.
dyk: In his first article in the radical magazine New Youth, published in April 1917, Mao urged readers to increase their physical strength to serve the revolution; his earliest poem to survive, "Changsha", was written on the eve of the Autumn Harvest Uprising of 1927.
ev: Mao Zedong is born near Shaoshan in Hunan, under the Qing dynasty
He is one of 13 delegates at the first congress of the Chinese Communist Party in Shanghai
The Red Army breaks out of the Jiangxi Soviet and begins the Long March
At the Zunyi conference Mao becomes de facto leader of the party and the Red Army
He proclaims the People's Republic of China from Tiananmen
He launches the Great Leap Forward, followed by the Great Chinese Famine
Mao dies, aged 82, and is succeeded at first by Hua Guofeng

sections.early:
Mao Zedong was born on 26 December 1893 near Shaoshan village in Hunan, during the Qing dynasty. His father, Mao Yichang, was a formerly impoverished peasant who had become one of the wealthiest farmers in Shaoshan; Mao described him as a stern disciplinarian who beat his children. His mother, Wen Qimei, was a devout Buddhist. At eight he was sent to the village school, where he disliked the Confucian classics and preferred novels such as Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Water Margin. At 13 his father married him to Luo Yixiu, aged 17, to unite their land-owning families; Mao refused to recognise her as his wife and became a fierce critic of arranged marriage.

On his father's farm he read voraciously, including translations of Adam Smith, Montesquieu, Rousseau and Darwin. In 1911 he began secondary school in Changsha, where he read Sun Yat-sen's newspaper and cut off his queue. When the Xinhai Revolution broke out he joined the rebel army as a private, without fighting, and left it in 1912. He then trained as a teacher at the Fourth Normal School of Changsha, where his professor Yang Changji introduced him to Chen Duxiu's magazine New Youth. He was elected secretary of the Students' Society in 1915, helped found the Renovation of the People Study Society in April 1918, and graduated in June 1919.
sections.rise:
In Beijing Yang Changji found him a post as assistant to the university librarian Li Dazhao, who added Marxism to the doctrines of the Chinese revolutionary movement; Mao, influenced also by Kropotkin's anarchism, moved towards Marxism over the winter of 1919. Back in Hunan he organised students and workers against the governor Zhang Jingyao and edited radical magazines. In 1921 he was one of 13 delegates at the first congress of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and became its secretary for Hunan. When the party allied with the Kuomintang (KMT), he rose to become the KMT's propaganda chief, and in 1924 a visit home convinced him of the revolutionary potential of the peasantry.

In 1927 Chiang Kai-shek turned on the Communists in the White Terror, and the CCP lost about 15,000 of its 25,000 members. Mao led the failed Autumn Harvest Uprising against Changsha and retreated with 1,000 survivors to the Jinggang Mountains, where he built a base, confiscated landlords' land and moulded his men, among them former bandits, into a disciplined force. Party leaders who held that only the urban proletariat could lead a revolution expelled him and ridiculed his peasant strategy. In 1934 the Red Army broke out of the encircled Jiangxi Soviet on the Long March; at Zunyi in January 1935 Mao became de facto leader of party and army, with Stalin's support. Only 7,000-8,000 of those who set out reached Shaanxi.
sections.deeds:
From Yan'an Mao proposed an alliance against Japan, and after the Xi'an Incident a United Front was formed with the KMT. The Red Army grew from 50,000 to 500,000, and Mao wrote Protracted Warfare and On New Democracy. When the civil war resumed after Japan's surrender in 1945, his forces defeated the Nationalist government, which withdrew to Taiwan, and on 1 October 1949 he proclaimed the People's Republic of China from Tiananmen.

In October 1950 he sent the People's Volunteer Army into the Korean War, in which at least 180,000 Chinese troops died. At home the party redistributed land and suppressed "counter-revolutionaries", and the government is credited with eradicating opium in the 1950s. The first five-year plan (1953-1958) brought rapid growth in heavy industry with Soviet help. Under the Two Bombs, One Satellite programme China built atomic and hydrogen bombs and became the fifth state with nuclear weapons, and from 1964 Mao pushed the Third Front, the building of industry in the interior.

In January 1958 he launched the Great Leap Forward to make China an industrial nation, merging collectives into vast people's communes. In 1966, fearing that a new elite had replaced the old and that the revolution was losing its zeal, he launched the Cultural Revolution to keep China in a state of "continuous revolution", with himself at the centre of a cult of personality.
sections.opponents:
Mao's rule was marked by mass killing and persecution. In the Futian incident of 1930 his loyalists tortured many and executed between 2,000 and 3,000 dissenters. In the land reform, people accused of being "landlords" and "rich peasants" were beaten to death at mass meetings; Mao claimed that 700,000 "counter-revolutionaries" were killed in 1950-1952, while estimates of the deaths range between 2 million and 5 million, and at least 1.5 million were sent to labour camps. He defended the killings as necessary to secure power. When critics spoke out in the Hundred Flowers Campaign, the Anti-Rightist Movement persecuted at least 550,000 people, mostly intellectuals.

In the Great Leap Forward cadres exaggerated harvests and requisitioned grain that did not exist, and the famine of 1959-1962 directly caused the death of some 30 million peasants. When Peng Dehuai criticised the policy at Lushan in 1959, Mao purged him; the CCP later concluded that as many as six million were wrongly punished in that campaign. Bernstein concludes that Mao "wilfully ignored the lessons" of the first phase. In the Cultural Revolution, Maurice Meisner gives about 400,000 deaths as a widely accepted minimum, and MacFarquhar and Schoenhals put those killed in rural China alone at 750,000 to 1.5 million. Li Rui, once on his secretarial staff, said that Mao "put no value on human life".
sections.last:
Mao stepped down as President in April 1959, keeping the chairmanship of the party and of the Military Commission, and in 1962 abandoned the Great Leap Forward; Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping rescued the economy by disbanding the communes. The Cultural Revolution destroyed much of China's cultural heritage and drove Liu Shaoqi among others to his death. Mao chose Lin Biao as his successor, but a divide opened between them, and on 13 September 1971 Lin died in a plane crash over Mongolia, presumably fleeing China; the CCP declared that he had planned to depose Mao. Mao declared the Cultural Revolution over in 1969, though many historians date its end to 1976. After President Richard Nixon's visit in 1972 relations with the United States improved.

His health declined in his last years, probably aggravated by chain-smoking, and his lung and heart ailments were kept a state secret. After heart attacks on 11 May, 26 June and 2 September 1976 he died shortly after midnight on 9 September, aged 82. His embalmed body lay in state in the Great Hall of the People for a week, and on 18 September a three-minute silence was observed across China. Despite his request to be cremated, his body was placed on display in the Mausoleum of Mao Zedong. He was succeeded first by Hua Guofeng, then in 1978 by Deng Xiaoping.
sections.legacy:
Mao has been called one of the most important and influential individuals of the 20th century. He is credited with ending decades of civil war, improving the status of women, literacy and education, a near doubling of life expectancy and the building of China's industry, and under him the People's Republic took China's permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council. His China has also been described as a totalitarian regime responsible for mass repression, and he as one of the great tyrants of the century. His theory of people's war still guides insurgents, and Maoism influenced the Khmer Rouge and Peru's Shining Path.

In 1981 the CCP's Resolution on party history held that his contributions far outweighed his mistakes, which it dated mainly from 1965; a common expression, first attributed to Deng Xiaoping, is that Mao was 70 percent right and 30 percent wrong. Chen Yun remarked that had Mao died in 1956 his achievements would have been immortal. In the West, Philip Short argued that a bit more than half of the deaths under Mao were unintended consequences of famine; Alexander Pantsov and Steven Levine called him "a successful creator and ultimately an evil destroyer"; Stuart Schram agreed with the Chinese view that his merits outweighed his faults while asking how land for peasants could be weighed against millions executed; and Maurice Meisner wrote that the era would still be recorded as one of the great modernising epochs in world history.

summary: Mao Zedong, born in Hunan in 1893, helped found the Chinese Communist Party, led it on the Long March and in 1949 founded the People's Republic of China. His campaigns, the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution cost tens of millions of lives, while he is also credited with ending civil war and with gains in literacy, health and national power.
references: Tim Clisson, Chinese Rules: Mao's Dog, Deng's Cat, and Five Timeless Lessons from the Front Lines in China (Harper, 2014)
Lee Feigon, Mao: A Reinterpretation (Ivan R. Dee, 2002)
Mobo Gao, The Battle for China's Past: Mao and the Cultural Revolution (Pluto Press, 2008)
Clare Hollingworth, Mao and the Men Against Him (Jonathan Cape, 1985)
Zhisui Li, The Private Life of Chairman Mao: The Memoirs of Mao's Personal Physician (Random House, 1994)
notes: Death place: the article does not say where Mao died; I gave no place.
He Zizhen: the article says 'In 1928, Mao met and married He Zizhen'; the marriages section says the two 'began a relationship' in 1928. I did not mention her marriage date.
The Futian incident is dated 'In December' after a November 1930 paragraph; I gave 1930. The proclamation of the Soviet Republic of China is dated only 'In November' and I left it out.

Death tolls: the article gives several figures that do not agree (the US State Department's 1976 estimate of a million in land reform and 800,000 in the counter-revolutionary campaign; 2-5 million; Mao's own 700,000). I gave the range and Mao's own claim, attributed. The famine figure 'some 30 million' is the article's, unattributed.
The 'Anti-Rightist' figures: the article says 'totalling perhaps 500,000' and 'at least 550,000'; I used the second.
Liu Shaoqi: the article lists him among the 'prominent figures' who 'perished in the violence of the Cultural Revolution'; I wrote that it 'drove Liu Shaoqi among others to his death'.
Present-day material in the article (polls of 2013 and later, Gen Z, surveys) left out as not lasting.

Wanted but not in the article: the place of death; the date he became President of the PRC; details of the Hundred Flowers Campaign's dates; the arrest of the Gang of Four beyond a mention; his relationship with Jiang Qing in the last years.
